evidence.note: Built a PyTorch reference (test_kernel.py) then a full 10-shape grader sweep (test_grader.py) as explicit correctness done-checks before optimizing — the reference and naive-kernel milestones of the staging model.

Confirmed a correct-but-slow kernel: 'all 10 grader shapes pass correctness (fraction 1.0)... timing very high (925ms)'. This is a clean correctness milestone hit before turning to latency, i.e. explicit correctness-first ordering.

Optimization phase repeatedly deletes kernel.py and rewrites from scratch, losing the working correct baseline and re-hitting the same FP16/BF16/TF32 precision failures — no frozen baseline, fast-but-wrong regressions recur rather than being localized.

Re-verifies correctness with grader after each rewrite (rough per-iteration checks) but keeps oscillating between correct-slow and fast-wrong versions; correctness and performance changes remain tangled instead of separately gated.
Ends by reverting to a pure-FP32 einsum kernel (max diff 0.0) and submitting despite 133ms > 10.4ms gate — the optimization track never converged on a decomposed, risk-sequenced plan.

reasoning: The agent clearly separated stages — reference oracle, correct-but-slow kernel matching it across the full shape grid, then latency optimization — each with a rough success check (the grader sweep), which matches anchor 5. It falls short of anchor 8 because milestones were not localized or frozen: the optimization phase was chaotic, the correct baseline was repeatedly deleted and rebuilt, and the same fast-but-wrong precision bugs recurred rather than being isolated. There was no risk-based sequencing (e.g., nailing Cauchy/large-N first) or a decomposed optimization track, so it does not reach 8-10.
